name: FAIR Data
title: FAIR Data
answer: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for making research data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable, published in 2016 as the FAIR Guiding Principles. It applies to data, metadata, code, samples and other research outputs, and it sits alongside open data as a related but distinct idea: data can be FAIR without being open, and open data is not automatically FAIR. In practice the principles shape how datasets are described, deposited and cited across disciplines, from genomics to social science, and they are now written into funder policies and journal requirements in many countries.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for making research data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable, published in 2016 as the FAIR Guiding Principles. It applies to data, metadata, code, samples and other research outputs, and it sits alongside open data as a related but distinct idea: data can be FAIR without being open, and open data is not automatically FAIR. In practice the principles shape how datasets are described, deposited and cited across disciplines, from genomics to social science, and they are now written into funder policies and journal requirements in many countries.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: FAIR data runs on persistent identifiers such as DOIs and ORCID iDs, metadata standards like Dublin Core and schema.org, and controlled vocabularies and ontologies that give terms stable meanings. Repositories, both general ones and discipline specific ones, provide the storage and the landing pages that make discovery and citation possible. Harvesting and cataloguing services aggregate metadata so that datasets can be found across sites, and machine readable licences state the terms attached to each item. None of this requires a single central system, which is both a strength and a source of fragmentation.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with planning: deciding what will be kept, what metadata will accompany it, and which repository fits the data and the funder's rules. Data is then cleaned, documented with a README or codebook, given a licence, and deposited with a persistent identifier, after which the record is cited in papers and linked to related outputs. Interoperability is handled by using common formats and vocabularies rather than bespoke ones, and reusability by describing provenance, methods and any access conditions. Much of the effort is unglamorous curation, and it is usually done by researchers, data stewards and repository staff together.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on consent, privacy, confidentiality and the terms set by funders, institutions and communities from whom data was collected. Personal and sensitive data can often be made FAIR through access controls, de identification or managed access rather than full release, and licences must be compatible with the underlying consent. Provenance matters because reusers need to know where data came from, how it was processed and who is accountable, and because attribution and credit depend on accurate records. Indigenous data sovereignty and other community governance frameworks set conditions that repositories and researchers are expected to respect, and getting this wrong can cause real harm even when the data is technically well described.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward machine actionable metadata, so that software agents can discover and assess datasets without a human reading every record, and toward closer links between data, code, models and publications. Assessment of FAIRness is maturing, with metrics and badges used by repositories and funders, though measuring compliance is easier than measuring genuine reuse. Tensions remain between openness and privacy, between global standards and local governance, and between the cost of curation and the funding available for it. Expect more emphasis on persistent identifiers, on provenance tracking for AI training data, and on treating data stewardship as a recognised professional skill rather than an afterthought.
